utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, do you recall testifying in the Krstic case on the 31st of May, 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to wrap it up again, we will admit the transcript as Exhibit P4051 and 11 expert reports as Exhibit -- from Exhibit P4052 to Exhibit P4062 and two associated exhibits as Exhibit P4063 and Exhibit P4064. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd now like to read out a summary of Dr. Lawrence's testimony from the Krstic case. In 1998, Dr. Lawrence oversaw the examination of human remains exhumed from eight Srebrenica-related mass graves; the Dam, Cancari Road 3, Cancari Road 12, Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5, Liplje 2, and Zeleni Jadar 5. He and his staff were based at the Gradska Groblja mortuary facility in Visoko. This facility had three autopsy tables, X-ray equipment, and a secure room for evidence storage. Later in the year, Dr. Lawrence's team also used two temporary mortuaries with additional autopsy tables to facilitate the processing of the remains. The human remains were delivered to the mortuary in body-bags and were held in a locked refrigerated container awaiting analysis. The analysis process started with the contents of the body-bag being photographed. The remains were then X-rayed using a portable X-ray machine known as a fluoroscope which was operated by a radiographer. The assigned pathologist would use the fluoroscope to look for fractures, bullets, any bony abnormalities and then prepare a handwritten report on his or her observations. The remains would then be taken to an autopsy table, where they were searched for personal items and clothing were removed. The clothing was tagged with the case number and handed to the scene of crime officer. The body was then washed and examined for injuries. Any obvious external injuries were photographed. The assigned pathologist would then conduct the autopsy and attempt to further define any areas of injury. They examined the bones for injury and in the case of apparent gun-shot injury, attempted to trace the track of the bullet. Anthropologists assisted with the interpretation of bone injuries, the calculation of sex, age, and the minimum number of individuals and the reconstruction of damaged bones. The pathologists also checked the clothing associated with a body to determine whether any defects in the clothing corresponded with the injuries on the body. During the autopsy the pathologists also looked for evidence of identifying features that may later help to identify the individual. Among the remains examined, Dr. Lawrence and his team found an individual with a grossly deformed ulna, an individual with severe sclerosis of the spine, an individual with tracheostomy, and other individuals with old unhealed fractures and severe joint damage caused by old gun-shot wounds. Lastly, the pathologist would prepare a handwritten report of his or her findings and form an opinion as to the cause of death. The report was typed up and signed by the pathologist and the body stored for hand-over to the Bosnian authorities. Dr. Lawrence prepared a report for each grave-site summarising these findings. In total, his team examined 2.239 body-bags, which, according to the anthropologists, contained a minimum number of 883 individuals. They identified 1.307 definite gun-shot wounds, six shotgun wounds and 25 shrapnel wounds, of which 24 came from the Zeleni Jadar 5 site. Fifty-three definite ligatures and as many as 83 ligatures were located. They also located 44 definite blindfolds and as many as 103. There were 254 relatively intact bodies among the remains examined. Of these, the cause of death of 50 was undetermined, one died of a combination of gun-shot and shrapnel wounds, and 203 died of gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, I now have some additional questions about your evidence. You discussed the morgue procedures at length in your Krstic testimony so I don't want to go through them in any detail. However, in your reports you described a change in procedure that took place during the season and in your reports for Liplje 2, Hodzici 3 and 5, and Zeleni Jadar there's a different in procedure. Can you explain that change in procedure and how it came about?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. As we got to about halfway through the season it became clear that because of the number of exhibits we were unlikely to complete the work in time unless we changed our procedure somewhat. It became increasingly clear to me that it was very difficult to interpret the material that we found in small body parts, isolated limbs and incomplete bodies. As a -- Mr. Jose Pablo, who was the chief anthropologist, proposed that we change how we did our work to concentrate on the larger body parts. It was important for the anthropologist to examine every bone because they needed to calculate the minimum number of individuals. So as a consequence, at the exhumation site, they divided the remains into isolated body parts, larger body parts, and large -- and almost complete bodies. The pathologists would examine the whole bodies and the larger body parts. The anthropologist would start examining the smaller body -- the isolated body parts. If the anthropologist found any injury, then they would be referred to a pathologist to have a complete report. So as a consequence, small body parts which were given -- were given a label of A were examined by the anthropologist. The larger body parts, and in particular things like skulls and so forth, were all examined by pathologists. And the whole bodies were examined exactly as they had been for the whole of the season.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In your reports we see you classify injuries that are identified on remains as either peri mortem, old post mortem or recent post mortem. Can you briefly describe those three terms.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. We were dealing with difficult remains. These were bodies that had old injuries that had started to heal or ante mortem injuries. They had injuries that had occurred at or around the time of death. They then had injuries that had occurred after death, but while the bones were still covered with flesh. And then in many cases they had injuries which had occurred once the bones had been stripped of flesh and had dried out. In order to distinguish between these, the wounds that were -- showed evidence of healing were classified as ante mortem. The injuries that occurred at the time of death were classified as peri mortem. The injuries that occurred in the bones while covered with flesh but apparently after the time of death were classified as early post mortem. And then the injuries that occurred once the bones were defleshed and dried were classified as late post mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to focus now on peri mortem injuries and specifically on gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 2471 in e-court, page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, when this picture comes up, I'd like you to, if possible, to use this picture to explain how a gun-shot wound was identified in a set of remains. And just while we're waiting this is the Cancari Road 12 site. Did you have an opportunity to go to that site?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I actually attended the site as well. Right. What you can see in the photograph -- sorry. There we go --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- one moment, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until assisted by our usher. So the witness wants to mark the picture so that if you could assist him with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, right. You can see this is a skull. It has been quite severely fractured, and then has been reconstructed by the anthropologist. When the skull was first received and was fragmented, it was very difficult to make out very much at all, but after it had been washed and reconstructed -- the white material you can see is glue that has been used to glue the fragments back together again. One can then see a defect here, which is where the bullet has entered the skull. You can see on the other side of this defect, it is irregular in shape and some of the small fragments of bone have been lost. On the other side of the skull over here you can see where the bullet has come out of the skull.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the future reference, could you put number 1 on the entrance part and number 2 for the exit part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Is this a definite gun-shot wound, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you give us just a brief example of something that you would have classified as a probable or a possible gun-shot wound? How would it differ from what we see here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In the skull, for example, if we had a similar radiating pattern of fractures but did not have all of the small fragments of bone which would enable us to define the entrance and the exit wound, that would be normally labelled as a probable gun-shot wound, provided we had metal fragments in the proximity of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what about a possible gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: We were dealing with bodies that were quite badly damaged and were quite disarticulated. There were some cases where we had fractures that looked suspicious to be gun-shot wounds but could not be defined as gun-shot wounds, but also had metal fragments in proximity to these and those I would describe them as possible gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Why did you consider it important to report probable and possible gun-shot wounds as well as the definite gun-shot wounds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Well, in some of the sites and particularly the Dam site and Liplje, there was so much damage that it was very difficult to ascertain exactly what was going on. The -- in those sites what we would do is apply our criteria for definite gun-shot wounds, and in both Liplje and in the Dam site there were relatively few cases which I would classify as definite gun-shot wounds. But I wanted to convey to the Court the idea that these were cases that may well be gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to ask you some questions about cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we keep this marking by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly put your initials and date of today, which is 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it separately, Exhibit P4065.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, we see in your reports that once an injury has been identified, depending on the injury, it can be classified as sufficient to cause death, a probable cause of death, possible cause of death, consistent with a cause of death, or in many cases the cause of death was undetermined. And I'd like to ask you to go through each of those categories and give us an example of an injury that would fit into each of those categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have up page 41 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when this picture comes up, Doctor, if you can use this as an example to explain how you categorise those injuries.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: You -- sorry, can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: You need to understand that many of these bodies were quite badly decomposed and were also disarticulated, that is, the body parts were no longer associated. In many cases the bodies were too decomposed to tell whether or not there was haemorrhage associated with the injury. In a few cases, and this example is one of them, the organs were well enough preserved to be absolutely certain what the cause of death was. This is a skull and it has been opened. What you can see under the skull is the brain and where the arrow is there is a bullet. On the outside of the brain there is black material which is decomposed blood. This is one of the few examples where one could be absolutely certain that the cause of death was a gun-shot wound of the head. In many of the others where the organs were not so well preserved, it was more difficult. In cases where you had a clear gun-shot wound in the head that had gone through the head, it was possible to say that this person had been shot and that this injury would cause death. Similarly in injuries in the chest, where there were bullet fragments or bullet tracts in the centre of the chest, even though the heart was no longer preserved it was pretty clear that a gun-shot wound of this nature would cause death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What kind of injuries would you classify as a probable or a possible cause of death?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In some of the others you had, for example, gun-shot wounds that were in the thigh. Now, a gun-shot wound in the thigh which may or may not strike the major artery, if it struck the artery or the bone, undoubtedly, left untreated, it would ultimately cause death. So in those cases we would give that as a probable cause of death. In some cases you had some evidence of gun-shot wound like small metal fragments close to organs that might cause death, but the injuries were so poorly defined that one couldn't be certain that that was a cause of death. And in those I might give the cause of death as being a possible -- as a possible cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In many cases you were unable to determine a cause of death at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. In the bodies where they were severely disarticulated and where we were not able to put the bodies back together again, we could not tell whether there was a real cause of death or not. In quite a few of these they did show some evidence of gun-shot wounds, and it is my belief that if we were able to put the bodies together again it might be possible to demonstrate a gun-shot wound. But because these were broken up and because we had no way at that stage of re -- of working out which body parts were associated, it wasn't possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please go back to page 40 of this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, is it possible to determine the time of death of these individuals from your pathological examination of their remains?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: From my pathological examination, no. The bodies had decomposed, but I cannot form any meaningful assessment of the time since death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a look at the third-last paragraph on this page, where you say: "Due to the degree of decomposition it is impossible to prove that any particular gun-shot wound was caused before or after death. However the pattern of shooting and the presence of objects such as blindfolds and ligatures as well as the attempts to conceal the bodies suggests to me that most of the shooting occurred at the time of death." Can you expand on this conclusion that you make in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said in -- when describing the case we previously saw of the gun-shot wound in the head, that was a very unusual case in which there was good preservation of the brain. And in that particular case one could be certain that that injury occurred at the time of death because of the haemorrhage. But in most cases, the decomposition of the body was such that one could not detect haemorrhage; and hence, you could not be certain that the injury occurred while the heart was still beating. Nevertheless, I would -- given that there were lots of gun-shot wounds in these bodies and given that there were blindfolds and ligatures on these bodies as well as the attempts that were clearly made to conceal the bodies, I think it's highly likely that the shootings occurred at the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the phrase "manner of death"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you please define that for us.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The manner of death is basically a legal concept of how the death came about. We typically talk about a natural manner of death or an unnatural manner of death, and then the manner of death in the unnatural might be divided into homicide, suicide, accident, misadventure, or perhaps in some cases where one cannot tell, an undetermined manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Is there a relationship between cause of death and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: To some degree, yes. One normally has to consider manner, but different systems deal with cause and manner slightly differently. I work in the Australian system which is very similar to the English coronial [sic] system, but I also did my training in the American system. Now in the Australian and English system it would be up to the coroner to assess the manner of death and the pathologist would normally define themselves to the cause of death. However, if you are doing an investigation of a death, the pathologist would usually make some form of assessment which would determine to what detail they go. For example, if I was dealing with a homicide in my own system, there would be certain things that I would do that I wouldn't routinely do for a natural death. So, to some degree, even in the English system or Australian system, a pathologist does have to consider manner of death. In the American system, the pathologist is called on to determine both the cause and manner of death. So, for example, in most of these sorts of cases the American pathologist would probably give the cause of death as gun-shot wounds and the manner of death as being homicide. Because I work in the Australian system and because most of my pathologists worked in the English-style systems, we gave cause of death but did not give manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: One final area, why did you record factors such as the absence of weapons and military uniforms in your reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I tend to record those things which I think might be alternative explanations for the material that I'm shown. Obviously in dealing with bodies that had come from a war zone, one of the alternative explanations for those bodies may well be that they were combat fatalities. It was therefore, I thought, important to record not only whether I thought there were ligatures and blindfolds, but also whether there was any evidence to suggest that these were, in fact, combatants. Other bits of information I also recorded, were any of these people wounded? We had one example of a man who had a shrapnel injury. The shrapnel injury had been bandaged and he had then been blindfolded and shot. And I considered all of these things as relevant to consideration of whether or not these were combatants or people who had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Very well. Doctor, your evidence in Krstic case was admitted in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for meeting with my legal advisor and for clarifying some things which I hope will help us to conduct this cross-examination smoothly and efficiently. Also, I would also like to acknowledge you for your moral integrity when in your country you noted an error and you publicly acknowledged it, admitted it. Can we look at 1D4 -- 1D4925. This error occurred in very good conditions for an autopsy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is a case that occurred 18 years ago and two of the three bodies were extremely badly burnt. I would not describe it as very good conditions for the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they better than the ones that you had in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In some ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to understand the relevance, could you explain a bit further why this is -- how this is relevant to our case, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think this simply shows that a pathologist, even an excellent one like Dr. Lawrence, can make a mistake and I think that is a relevant information for the Chamber when considering his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1977. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you something about insects. Are you knowledgeable about insects and their behaviour as far as corpses or mortal remains are concerned? Is that something that you took into account?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I am -- I'm a forensic pathologist, not an entomologist. I have dealt with some cases where forensic entomology has been concerned and I do have a working knowledge of forensic entomology, but I would not claim to be an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that field applicable to the cases that you worked on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I did not see very much evidence to support that. In one of the graves, and I think it was CR12, we did see some very small maggots. And I think that what those maggots represent is a re-infestation of the body after exhumation. But I did not see any evidence of things like pupal cases or other evidence of previous insect infestation that would, I think, assist in assessing time since death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about skeletisation, would that indicate something? Would various degrees of body decomposition indicate anything about that and does skeletisation indicate the presence of insects or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The process of decomposition can occur with or without insects, and similarly the process of skeletisation can occur with or without insects. The -- some of the bodies that we saw showed quite a lot of -- a decompositional process that we call adipocere. Now, this is a process that occurs when a buried body is exposed to water and is a process of formation of free fatty acids which stop bacterial proliferation. Decomposition can occur without insects but can be due to bacterial growth alone. So I don't think that the presence of skeletalisation [sic] necessarily indicates the involvement of insects. It could easily do so and the evidence has now gone, but I did not see anything apart from the small number of maggots which I did see in CR12, which would indicate the presence of insects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the presence of insects give any kind of indication as to the time that the body was there from the time of death to the time of burial?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, if they were present it could be helpful. I think my experience with forensic entomology suggests to me that sometimes it's helpful and sometimes it's not. It doesn't always work. I also suspect that after three years quite a lot of the forensic entomology evidence would have gone and would not be recoverable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will leave that topic then. Can you please tell us whether Serbian pathologists took part in this. I'm speaking of Republika Srpska as one of the interested parties there.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information in advance about where you were coming, what was happening there earlier, whether you had information about the fact that war was waged in that area for 44 months?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I had been briefed at the ICTY and I was aware that war had been fought in that area for some period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you warned, were you instructed about the possibility of encountering graves that were there considerably earlier than July 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Not specifically, but obviously I considered that a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I can see in your report here for Hodzici 5, this is 65 ter 2475, page 3, where you say that officers at the scene of the crime were looking for objects on the basis of which it could be determined that the persons were coming from Srebrenica. So there was an awareness then that some people were not originally or were not coming from Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. I think the reason that they were looking for identification was to establish whether they did come from Srebrenica. I don't think it was assumed they came from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was attention drawn in any way to the possibility of some of the grave-sites dating back to a period before July of 1995 and was the area where combat took place and where these grave-sites from an earlier period were possibly located identified?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: You must remember, I was dealing with the mortuary side of this, not the exhumation side of this. Those questions are probably better put to Professor Wright than to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did put that question to him. What I wanted to ascertain was it says here in the introduction that between 12 and 20 July exhumations were conducted, but you did not attend any of these exhumations or did you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I -- my main job was to run the mortuary and I had to be there in the mortuary when it was working. I have known Professor Wright for a long period of time and I am interested in attending the scenes if I can, and I did, in fact, attend the sites of Cancari Road 12, Cancari Road 3, Liplje, and also Zeleni Jadar but not when they were actually digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we have this document pulled up, can we have page 2, please. This concerns at least 57 individuals of whom 54 were ascertained to have been male. Let me not read all of it. We can all see this for ourselves. Can I direct your attention to item 4. There you say that there were 31 blindfolds recovered, 19 of which were around the head, two on other parts of the body, two were associated with bodies in general but their exact location was not stated by the pathologist. And eight were loose in the grave. You say the fabric of some ligatures was similar to other Hodzici sites. Was this something you did yourself or did you authorise some of your associates to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The similarities between the blindfolds were fairly obvious. I did examination of these to ascertain whether I thought they were similar. These blindfolds were then sent to The Hague to see -- to -- in case further examination by an expert was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you carry out these autopsies or some of your associates? Because you say there that the location was not stated by the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have carried out probably around maybe a fifth of the examinations, maybe a quarter. I'm not exactly sure. Some -- the pathologists who were involved - and there were usually three pathologists until later in the season when there were up to five -- so I was in the -- in the mortuary. I examined probably around about 20 per cent or so of the cases. But other cases were being examined which I would review but did not directly carry out myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But elsewhere in your reports you said on several occasions that every pathologist who carries out an autopsy stands by his findings; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, you took care of some sort of standard, whereas the actual autopsy work, the findings and interpretations, were theirs; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. When we -- when they came, I would brief them on what we were doing, what I needed them to do, and that included discussions about identification of gun-shot wounds, identification of ligatures and blindfolds. They -- they would write the report in their own words, and in some cases they did not provide a description in their report of where the blindfold was found. So in those cases I listed them as being exact site undetermined. Now, I have to say I did examine the blindfolds, particularly later when -- at The Hague as well -- and we did measure them and they were all quite similar. In particular in Hodzici, this particular site Hodzici Road 5, there was one blindfold which was made from a leg of a pair of trousers which I realised was identical and could be matched up to a blindfold that was recovered from Hodzici Road 4. So while I could not tell -- if the pathologist didn't record where the blindfold or ligature was, I did examine the blindfold and ligature to ascertain whether or not in form and material it was similar to the ones we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 15 and then 16 in Serbian. I think the same applies to the other version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The table of blindfolds recovered at the HZ5 site, the number, material, width, circumference, and location. So we have 31 blindfolds, 19 around the head, two, et cetera.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There was a -- I can show you it. I -- I -- I'm not an expert on fabric, but I can show you what it looked like. It was a shiny material which did not have a flat surface, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Chamber request that the Prosecution provide us with the blindfolds after the break.

utterances.text: Do you have a picture in colour -- probably in one of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.text: This is one of the ligatures and you can see --

utterances.text: Just hold on. Can we zoom in a bit further. Yes.

utterances.text: You can see here that is the head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Probably you need to push the button on that -- just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not going to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until assisted by our -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. This is the head here and this is the blindfold here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is that the back of the head or the face that we are seeing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's a really good question. I think it might be the front, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Don't you think we would be able to see the nasal cavity and the mouth cavity if it were the face?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Possibly, but with the adipocere that was present a lot of the facial features have been lost. I cannot tell you looking at that whether we are looking at the face or the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if the face were concealed, turned the other way, then we wouldn't be able to say with any certainty where the blindfold is exactly resting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the -- the face is here, but I agree that it is hard for somebody who did not see this thing to assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Doctor, would the adipocere also cover the teeth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: It would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may do, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is it the time for our break? I'm asking lest I should continue my examination -- or perhaps one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This particular pink blindfold does not -- is it a jeans-made blindfold? It doesn't seem to have -- we don't know about the pattern.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This particular one is -- yes, is a pat -- is a fabric that I did not see -- I only saw once. If we turn the page, though, I can show you the pink shiny material.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to admit this and keep this or it won't be necessary? I leave it in your decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do believe it's already -- well, yes, I do agree. It can be marked for identification. We haven't really identified where the face or where the back of the head are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I don't think -- I don't think Dr. Lawrence marked a very significant marking here, so we can continue. Yes, we move -- we will not keep this separately. Would you like to ask that question before the recess or shall we take the recess -- the break now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take the break. I will ask the witness to show us what the typical blindfolds were and that will entail a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If Dr. Lawrence could take -- consider that and come up with -- some examples after the break, I would appreciate it very much. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at something we were trying to see before, page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the e-court have some problem? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 15 in English and 16 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, does this not seem pretty uniform to you, pink embossed, pink embossed, pink embossed scalloped edges? Can we now have the next page in English. Page 16 of this document in English. Do you remember, Dr. Lawrence, that many of these blindfolds did not have any knots and where they did it would be indicated -- no, this isn't the page that I'm asking for. I'm looking for page 16 with text. The Serbian can stay as it is and I'd like a page in English which relates to that same site, HZ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page 21. Were you referring to this page, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should have a table on it. It should appear the same as the Serbian page. So page 14, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it not the case that only two are indicated here as having had a knot, whereas all the other ones have no knot, they seem to have been made of one piece?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There are two in which there is a knot halfway in the middle making two loops, but most of these were single loops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the previous page in English where it states and I'll read in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

It may be the page before in English where fabric is described, four types of fabric. Pink colour of salmon, shiny like satin with multi-coloured floral pattern, light blue material akin to satin. Can we have the English page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just next page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In e-court next page. Serbian was okay. In English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's the next page on in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It appears to be a fabric of some luxury, it appears to be an expensive one, does it not, Dr. Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you acquainted with our customs of war and our religious and cultural customs before they brought you to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the last two men, one has civilian clothes and a rifle and the other one has something over his mouth, it's a band covering his mouth, but he does have something on his forehead as well.

utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'm not going to pursue this further, although we have a few more video-clips. I'm going to show that on some other occasion. utterances.text: I wasn't aware that that was the custom, no.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? We will provide the exact minute references. The case manager, or rather, my associate is going to take care of that.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I would not necessarily anticipate that a soldier would be buried with their weapons. I do understand that a previous soldier from 2000 -- sorry, 1997 was found to be carrying a hand-grenade, but I understand that it would be fairly unlikely for the person to be buried with a weapon. We did look for ammunition and we did find occasional pieces of ammunition, I think three pieces in total, none of which looked like contemporary military ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You found that in the pockets, right, or in the handbags?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE

utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I'm working on right now. I do apologise. Just a moment.

utterances.text: My reading of my own report indicates that the ligature photographed is described as being a ligature. HZ05B091 was recovered with his hands tied behind his back with a 4-millimetre-wide cord tied to form two loops. 120 and 130 millimetres in circumference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 13 in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Possibly it was somewhere else in one of your other findings, perhaps this doubt was expressed, but it doesn't really matter now. Let us go back to page 2. What is stated here is that some bodies were better preserved than in other locations. And that some bodies were more intact and 51 of 57 bodies were totally intact. The intact bodies show that there was little disturbance during the second burial. How do you explain the second burial? Does that mean adding bodies to an already-existing grave or had these people been buried somewhere else and then re-buried into this grave? Or rather, let's put it this way, according to your findings were there people there who were -- who had been buried at different points in time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, if you're talking about the appearances of them in the grave, those are questions that are better put to Professor Wright. I did attend some of these graves, but I certainly cannot attest to those sorts of things. It is one of Professor Wright's areas of expertise, not mine. There is -- the Hodzici Road bodies were well -- were surprisingly intact. They did vary in their degree of decomposition and this is a feature that one sees in forensic pathology. There is often a great deal of variation in how fast a body can decompose. In addition, work done on mass graves from the Second World War demonstrates that. On the outside of the grave the bodies decompose faster than on the inside of the grave simply because of proximity to air, to water, and that in the centre of the grave one tends to see less decomposition because there is less oxygen. So a degree of variation is not at all uncommon in a mass grave. What is a little unusual in Hodzici 5 is how well preserved they are. And I -- I personally cannot explain why they are that well preserved. I think it is a feature under which the bodies were and also to some degree if the body is not disrupted it won't decompose as quickly. So, yes, Hodzici 5 is unusual. Why is it unusual, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked that only because of this paragraph here, 7 and 8, especially 8, where there is a reference to the second burial. That is why I asked that, but basically you cannot answer that; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. I -- if you look at the patterns in the primary and secondary graves, there are some features that suggested -- but again, Professor Wright is the expert that you should be talking to about the intactness of the bodies and the circumstances. He was the one who exhumed them. He would know the answers to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the degree of decay is a matter for pathologists; right? Can the time be established, the time of death and the time of burial --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- on the basis of the degree of -- all right. Thank you. On this page we see that it is believed that there is some likelihood of a person to have suffocated. Do you exclude the possibility that this body had -- was lying facing some dirt surface and that that is how the dust and dirt got in?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. The pathologist thought that there was soil in the trachea, in the airway down a long way from the mouth. I had a look at the case and I was not convinced that the soil had necessarily got there in life. There was a small defect in the trachea and I think that the soil could have fallen in there after death. So I was not convinced -- it's possible, but I was not convinced that it was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to appear on the next page, one fairly intact body had an undetermined cause of death, possibly suffocation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Again ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the pathologist gave -- suggested that that was a possibility. I looked at the case and was not convinced, but I -- I have listed what the pathologist said rather than what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, an archaeologist cannot speak of the time of death. Can a pathologist, though, speak of time of death; and if so, under which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: As I get older, I find myself more and more uncertain about assessing time since death. I am reluctant to do it even in fresh bodies and I'm even more reluctant to do it in decomposed bodies. I have been fooled before and I don't think that I can, as a general principle, make a strong assessment of time since death based on just examination alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at page 8 in Serbian. Perhaps it's page 7 in English. It says "findings, post mortem findings." And that is precisely what you are speaking about. You are speaking about different degrees of decomposition and decay to total skeletisation. That cannot really help in determining when a person died and was buried?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This finding here, is that your own finding or the finding of the pathologist? And how could he come to the conclusion that this had nothing to do with the time of death or --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, are we talking about paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After paragraph 4: [In English] "This group of bodies was the best preserved. [B/C/S spoken] The variation in decomposition between the sites appeared to reflect local conditions in the primary and secondary grave, and not any difference in time since death."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if there was no primary and secondary grave, if one grave is primary as a whole and if it has this range of changes, does that mean that bodies were added to that grave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that is a possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Look, again, Richard Wright was the one who did the exhumations. Those questions should be put to him, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you as a pathologist. When you see this kind of range in terms of the decay of bodies, a pathologist is in a position to speak about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I can -- there are lots of factors that would alter the decomposition, how long they've been dead for, whether they've been buried or exposed to the air, if they're in a mass grave or a single grave, the temperature, the soil moisture, the degree of breakdown of the body, access to insects. There are multiple reasons for the variation. What I'm saying here is that I think that in view of the location of the mass grave the variation in decomposition is probably explained. But I accept that I cannot ascertain, myself, the time since death, and so there are alternative explanations possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that Mr. Wright also said that we should talk to a pathologist as far as the decay of bodies is concerned, so obviously we'd have to have a group seance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked the question to Mr. Wright and that's nothing to do with this witness. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at page 10 in Serbian, peri mortem injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about injuries inflicted by fire-arms, gun-shot wounds, and you're talking about three criteria, three elements, in terms of establishing whether something is a gun-shot wound. Are these the only criteria involved or is it possible that there may be some other criteria as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No, there are other criteria. These are the criteria that we -- I talked to the pathologist about in these particular bodies. In a normal well-preserved body, we wouldn't have any of these problems. If the skin's present, we normally have bullet-holes in the skin, we have the bullet, it's fairly easy. Because these bodies are quite decomposed, some of them have a bit of skin and when there is skin it makes it much easier. But a lot of these bodies didn't have all of the skin and so I had to talk to the pathologist about the other criteria that they would use to assess this. The first one is finding the bullet in the soft tissue or the bone. The second one is finding the hole that the bullet made in the body. And the third one is where you've got small fragments of metal from a bullet on the X-ray and fractures along the -- and fractures in the adjacent bone. Again, if the body were fully preserved, I wouldn't need -- wouldn't normally apply these criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 14 in Serbian, bullets and bullet fragments recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There you conclude that due to skeletisation and the fact that clothing was underground, it was impossible to establish the distance from which fire was opened; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. Assessing range of fire pathologically you look for evidence of either -- if the gun's held in contact, a muzzle abrasion, and soot within the wound; and it's a little bit further away up to a metre, you look for gun powder stippling on the clothing or on the body; and if it's further than that you can't really tell. As a pathologist all I can tell is whether a gun's been held in contact with the skin, between 0 and a metre, and then further than a metre. Now, in this particular case there was so much soil -- first of all, with no tissue I couldn't tell whether the range of fire was contact or not. There just wasn't enough tissue to be certain. Then in regards to the intermediate range there was a lot of clothing present and the clothing was very heavily soiled. I did see one case and I think it was in -- range of fire -- sorry. Oh, it's not -- there was one case in which I thought I could see gun powder residue, and that piece of clothing was sent to The Hague in case they wanted to do testing on it. In general I felt that it was -- and as a -- I should say, it is my standard practice when dealing with ordinary cases to examine the clothing for gunpowder residue just to try and ascertain that. In this particular case we needed to clean the clothing to examine it. We also were hoping to use the clothing to identify the individuals. So I made a decision to clean the clothing, which is not standard practice, in order to do that. Having said that, I only saw one case where I thought there was evidence of gunpowder stippling and I was looking for it. I accept that the cleaning of the clothing would make it difficult to ascertain range of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You observed and noted quite a few gun-shot wounds to legs and feet. Did you have any sort of explanation for that? Can a pathologist account for how such injuries came about?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Can I have the image in CR12 of the -- after page number 11.

utterances.text: I do have, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's after page number 11.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the image marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit Number D1978. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was no explanation provided by the pathologist on the nature of these injuries; right? Can a pathologist address these issues?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Possibly. I must admit, it was when I started looking at the sum total of all of the cases from CR12 that I thought it was unusual and it took me to the particular case if we can find it. So that's a body diagram with a number of X-rays around it and circles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's the photograph that's after page 11 in the report -- well, it's [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the hard copy, you have just a blank page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have a very poor quality of it, Mr. President. But perhaps, Doctor, if you could demonstrate the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could put it on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excellent. Okay. Now, having looked at the -- having looked at the overall diagrams, this is one of the cases that I did myself. And it's got an odd pattern of gun-shot wounds. There seems to have -- there seems to be deliberate targeting of the joints, the knees, the wrists, the shoulders, and then the fatal gun-shot wound is in the head. As a pathologist I never use the term "torture," but one wonders if these injuries were not deliberately inflicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to find out whether this is included in his report or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can read out what I've said. Figure -- figure 2: "There were bullet fragments and gun-shot wounds in the left shoulder, right upper arm, right and left elbow, right hand, left forearm, right knee, and left lower leg, as well as a fatal gun-shot wound in the head. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It is in his report, Mr. President, but I think the copy in e-court might have been uploaded incorrectly and that particular page, certainly my copy, is just plain black and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, in e-court it is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- we will fix it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we cannot state with any certainty that this was not scattershot fire opened while the individual was fleeing and moving his arms and legs about. This is something we cannot rule out; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: It's -- I don't know what it means, but I have to say I saw it in that grave but not in the other graves. It's the only three cases where I suspected it and, you're right, I don't know exactly how it came to -- occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the old document again, page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let us find the passage in the report first. Are we on the correct page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The page -- it's 13 in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
