utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there it is. Were you told -- was there a suggestion made to you that all these individuals were prisoners or people captured who were executed in the month of July of 1995 or were you also given a possibility that these were grave-sites dating back to various periods and various seasons?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No, I was told that there were prisoners who were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we are on page 22 I guess, but where do we find that passage, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The penultimate paragraph, peri mortem injuries, the clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Many of the bodies were wearing two or three layers" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't think that they were fair in their dealings with you, Dr. Lawrence, because a war lasted in that area for 44 months and there were around 50 Serbian mass graves, but we dug them up in 1993 when we liberated the area. Do you agree that it is far more likely that these individuals were killed in winter rather than in summer in the month of July?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: They were wearing multiple layers of clothing. Why they were wearing multiple layers of clothing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have -- it's page 18 in my copy and the chapter is "Cause of Death" on the previous page and interested in the one that follows from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to be clear we are back to Hodzici Road number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time to go through all the 11 documents. That's simply because I haven't -- been given enough time, but let's look at two or three of them to see what sort of limitations were confronted in this sort of work. Can we look at something that I have at the top here, [In English] HZ05B175. [Interpretation] There bullet fragments were found in the heart. Elsewhere a pathologist who worked on the -- the pathologist who worked on the body said that in his view the individual had suffocated as there had been no change in the body --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let us find the page and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The title of the chapter is "Cause of Death." And then the following page --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we find that? It's page 18 in the copy I have, so it must be 16 were perhaps a higher number, cause of death, yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page, please. In English it reads: B175, that's the third paragraph from the bottom, was a fairly intact body in a moderate state of preservation. "There was no evidence of gun-shot wounds ... and soil was observed in the trachea ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page? In the Serbian version, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There it says that bullet fragments were recovered from the heart. It's the third paragraph from the top. It says B175 [In English] "... a bullet fragment is recovered in the heart. The cause of death is certain."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that would -- that would appear to be an error there. I -- if you look at the listing at the back where I go through all of the gun-shot -- all of the cases, there are no gun-shot wounds in 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're on this page let's deal with the following. You say that due to the degree of decomposition in most of these cases it was impossible to ascertain if a certain wound was inflicted by fire-arms before or after death; right? That is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, except for the case that I showed you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English and can we have the bottom of the Serbian page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "There were parts of 57 individuals ..." And you say that since individual bodies cannot be reconstructed I stated the cause of death for each body-bag rather than each individual. It is possible that a divided individual where head and torso are separate, that more than one cause of death was stated; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to page 14, or rather, we've done with the clothing -- I'm sorry, we've done with that, we've finished with that. Can we have the last textual page. The other features that may help identify a body.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at all the various items found on these individuals. B116: Pen, razor blades, notes, glasses, purse, papers, handkerchief. B153: Watch, key, metal box, purse, jewellery. B154: Personal papers. B156: Fob watch, prayer beads. B160: Prayer beads, knife, coins, key. And the penultimate, B169: Watch, earrings, flintstone, and the last one, ring loose in jacket. This is what the pathologist found when the bodies were brought in?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have a look at table 6, provisional identification of bodies. Let's look at identity papers. Is it not stated here that identity cards were found even two on one individual?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I told you that it was a custom in our parts whereby a prisoners would not be able to have any valuables in his pocket because he would be able to bribe someone and he wouldn't be able to have any identity papers on them, do you agree that these individuals having had their documents were not taken prisoner -- were not prisoners of war before their death?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain this to you. In respect of this grave-site, you were told that these were individuals who were previously taken prisoner in July of 1995 and were then executed. I put it to you that these individuals were killed when it was winter-time and that they were not previously taken prisoner because prisoners of war cannot retain identity papers or valuables because that would make flight easier for them. Does this not sound to you as a possibility as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment one way or the other on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Doctor didn't testify that these individuals were taken prisoner and then executed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he did confirm that directions were given to him to the effect that these were individuals who were taken prisoner in Srebrenica in July of 1995 and that they were executed. And he was given that suggestion. It was not his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered he cannot comment one way or the other on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the interview with my advisor, Mr. Robinson, you said that a conclusion cannot be drawn as to whether the deaths or the dead bodies from a grave-site came from one war episode or several and that no conclusion can be drawn to the effect that they were all killed or died at the same time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that's exactly what I said. I think what I said was that, looking at the pattern of gun-shot wounds, I cannot reach any conclusion regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in these reports that there is no prevalent position or direction from which bodies were fired at?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. I have tried -- we've tried quite hard to assess the direction of fire, and the problem is for everyone that I can work out the direction there are probably two or three where I can't work out the direction. So I think it would be extremely dangerous to draw any conclusion about that. If I knew -- if I had perfectly well preserved bodies and I knew the direction of fire, I might be able to draw some conclusion. But in this particular case a majority of them I can't tell the direction of fire. So I think it would be extremely dangerous to draw any conclusion from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you said that you cannot conclude whether these are fighters or non-fighting men, right, on the basis of the remains that you examined?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, I can't conclude whether they're fighters or non-fighters on the basis of the injuries. I think that people with blindfolds and ligatures are probably not combatants at the time that they're shot. There are clearly old people with severe disabilities amongst these people who are unlikely to be combatants. There are also young people who I think are unlikely to be combatants. If -- if these were combatants, why did somebody go to so much trouble to conceal the graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that people who had several layers of clothing on them were in secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that the persons that I'm speaking about who had several layers of clothing on, are you sure that their bodies were being concealed? As a pathologist could you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. The nature -- ascertaining whether a grave was a secondary or a primary grave was not my function. That was, again, a function of Professor Wright.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if we do not deal with that as pathologists, right, we cannot know whether they had been buried several times, right, that is something that a pathologist cannot tell on the basis of the remains he has on his table?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The answer to that's both yes or no. There were -- there was damage to the bones which I think had occurred after death which I don't normally see in the -- in buried bodies that I normally deal with. And I think does suggest some component of damage during excavation. But as I said, it wasn't my role to ascertain which was a primary and a secondary grave. Other people were doing that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you said that the number of wounds on one's body was not indicative in any way in terms of whether the victim had died in combat or not, right? Although you do say that most of the injuries came from automatic or semi-automatic weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, I think we were seeing many less gun-shot wounds than were actually present. There were a number of cases where we had multiple gun-shot wounds close together in a line which I think would be consistent with an automatic weapon, and that's about all I can really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you confirmed that it was not possible to establish the time between death and burial; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that not possible or is that not something you had said?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I don't think it was reasonably possible, given the time that they'd been -- the decomposition and the time they'd been dead for. Those sorts of things would require something like forensic entomology or something to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your position is that in Bosnia most garments were not sent for ballistic examinations, although that would have been done under normal circumstances. You say that garments had been washed and you say that it would have been better had the wounds been examined; right? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is in Australia we would probably have sent -- well, I'm not sure all of the garments, but some of the garments to be examined. Having said that, I'm not a ballistics expert and I don't know how successful you can be examining gun-shot residue in a body that's been buried for three years. I suspect that it's probably less successful than if it was fresh, but I don't know. The other thing was that we did not have a ballistics lab in Bosnia at the time. And also that in fact that we were using the clothing to try and identify who these people were. And so for a lot of reasons we did not do something that I might do back in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, please. Cancari and the Cancari Road location 3, 1998, it says here there were many wounds --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have a reference. We cannot find this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you slow down. If you would like to put a question in relation to that report, we'll upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The ERN number is 00920597 and that is the Cancari road, location 3. It's on page 2 in the document that I have. 12, 2472, that is the 65 ter number. I don't know what the P number is but the 64 -- 65 ter number was 2472 and then it's page 2. P4056. Yes, location 3. Next page, please, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your conclusion or his? Do you know who it was that was carrying out the post mortem in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, which -- which -- the summary was mine. Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He referred to para 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Para 12. These were -- these were my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can one conclude this, Dr. Lawrence, unless you were under pressure to explain everything?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. I'm a -- I'm a forensic pathologist. I have a little experience with anthropology. The fractures we're talking about here were of a type that occur after death with dried bone. They do not look like peri mortem injuries at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that would mean that someone had dug up the corpse, broken the bones, and then returned it so that people would be fooled once an exhumation takes place. Is that the only explanation or is there another plausible explanation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No, no, it could have occurred during our exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at -- oh, all right, this has to do with -- actually, page 24, can we have a look at 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Many bodies here also had two or three layers of clothes; right? I have page 24. Yes. This is what I have here, many bodies, yes, yes. It's page 12 here, I assume. The top of the page, please, in English?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The top of both pages, please, in e-court, the very beginning of both pages. So in this grave many bodies were also wearing two or three layers of clothing; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at the bottom of the page, B319, B319. The damage here was consistent with being chewed by a dog; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to what was concluded here, is it possible that this bag had not been buried for a long time generally speaking? Before being buried the body was on the ground for a long time, accessible to animals, and then it was found and then it was buried. That possibility cannot be ruled out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 32 in Serbian, again it's 319, there is part of a wire and your comment is: "I'm not convinced that this had been a ligature." CR03B319.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, there was -- I think in a couple of the graves there were a few pieces of wire and I don't know what they are. I couldn't -- I couldn't in my own mind convince myself that they were ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 53 in Serbian. There are other marks of identification here, old injuries, et cetera, and also other things that were found, cigarette boxes with dedications and things like that. That had also been found; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you found here was that there were quite a few wounds that were inflicted by shells; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few had old gun-shot injuries which were healing -- which were healed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this lead you to believe that this was a fighter who had been wounded earlier on as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what it means. It means that it had an old gun-shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will I get more time, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the distinguished Dr. Lawrence handed in 11 reports and I've just touched upon two. So I don't know whether this is exemplary in terms of showing what the constraints are and especially the constraints imposed by the hosts, not explaining to Dr. Lawrence that there had been a war going on there in that area for 44 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has been put and answered. In realistic terms, how much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, it depends on what I'm expected to do, whether I'm expected to go through each and every report with Dr. Lawrence before you or should I just dwell on particular examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for you how to conduct your cross-examination, but it's time to wrap up your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well then I'm not going to have enough time to deal with many things. I won't be able to show many things because these are 11 expert reports. It is a fortunate circumstance that I am a doctor as well and that I can read these reports, but there are 11 reports after all. Two hours, two and a half hours is too little time for me for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break now for an hour, after which you will have a half an hour, Mr. Karadzic, to conclude your cross-examination. We'll resume at 1.40. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to your findings related to Zeleni Jadar, location 5. Let us just briefly take a look at a few things there. On page 2 there is a reference to different stages of decomposition, and then yet again there is this explanation stating that it seems that the difference between locations reflects local conditions in primary and secondary graves, not the difference in time that had elapsed from the death involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have an exact reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this an example of the rule that this would not be the only explanation --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- that is paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 2476 is the 65 ter number, but I don't know what the P number is. You found quite a few gun-shot wounds and in 24 you found bodies with gun-shot wounds -- you found gun-shot wounds, you found shrapnel wounds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, 24 shrapnel wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And gun-shot wounds too, right, those are hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know -- sorry, you mean shot-gun -- yes, sorry. Yes, we had gun-shot wounds, we had 24 shrapnel wounds, and we had four shot-gun wounds. Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 it says: "One of the shot-gun wounds to the lower legs appeared to be bandaged ..." So that means that the person was wounded first and bandaged and then died -- rather, lost his life; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 15, the conclusion is that it is not possible to guarantee that in a single bag there were only the body remains of one person and again the causes of death are listed for the body-bags not for each and every individual --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this -- does this bring into question, or rather, interfere with the estimated number of victims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. This -- again, this question should probably be put to Mr. Baraybar, but my understanding is that they looked at the number of the bones and so therefore it should not interfere too much with this estimation of numbers. But again, Mr. Baraybar is the expert to which you should put those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you to tell us how many post mortems can be carried out by a forensic expert? What would be the maximum or minimum or what would be the optimum? The minimum would be one or none. So I'm talking about such cases as well as fresh corpses.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I -- in a day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the course of a seven-hour workday.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: It depends on -- on what you need to achieve. In a disaster-type situation where you're only trying to examine for evidence of identification, you could do a lot more. In a case where you're dealing with homicide, I think it takes a bit longer. Generally speaking, I would do somewhere between four and maybe six in a day. Obviously I'd got a little bit more experienced by the time I'd finished, but it depends a little bit on the experience of the pathologist to some degree and also on how extensive the remains were. The more skeletalised they were the more the anthropologist might do rather than the pathologist. But, for example, with a fairly intact body, it might take an hour or so to do the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at "Post Mortem Findings," that chapter. In Serbian it's page 12. You've probably found it and could it be found for the sake of the other participants as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English version on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does the first part read, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Level of preservation, decay, and then there are five paragraphs, and then there is the subheading also in bold and then below it says decay or decomposition. I have page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think it's page 8, Mr. President, it's -- ends with the ERN 7975.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well please help us understand this, Dr. Lawrence. So relatively well-preserved with skin, about 25, and then in 83 body-bags partial skeletonisation and then 51 body-bags largely or completely skeletonised. And then in 21 cases the degree of preservation was not adequately described to classify. And then paragraph 5, paragraph 5, what is stated here is [No interpretation] and in two cases there was a description of mummification.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would you say as a pathologist? What would you conclude as a pathologist? What would you tell us? How can there be such a degree of variety in a single grave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Because there is. No, you -- the conditions in a grave, a mass grave, can vary from top to bottom. Adipocere, for example, is a process which requires water. So in the bottom of a grave one might well expect adipocere. At the top of the grave if the material is, well, draining you might get drying out of the body. So it's possible to get both mummification and adipocere depending on the amount of moisture present. As I also described previously, in the mass graves, you often go from the outside where you have got almost complete loss of the tissue to the inside where there's no oxygen where you get almost entirely preserved bodies. So the answer is you can get that sort of variation in one grave. As I have said, it's one explanation for the -- for that the -- there are possibly other explanations for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would imply that the time of death has to be estimated, the time of burial, the time that a body would spend outside a grave; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. There are other explanations for the observation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at page 19, that is what I have, so that is peri mortem wounds, shot-gun, shrapnel, let us just have a look at the variety involved, the variety of fragments. In English can we find the right version as well. On the previous page you said that not a particular direction prevailed. You do remember having said that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the distribution of shrapnel is rather diversified. Different parts of the body, the right hip, the chest, the neck, pelvis, et cetera. Would you agree that this indicates a war operation, or rather, combat?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that just looking at the wounds, the shrapnel wounds themselves, I could tell the difference between combat or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it does resemble combat a great deal, does it not? It is difficult to shoot someone with shrapnel, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to execute someone with a shell, i.e., by shrapnel. So it is more likely that this was the case of combat? Or rather, let me put it this way, can combat be regarded as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Shrapnel injuries are more common as a form of -- a cause of death than gun-shot wounds, yes. In this particular instance can I tell from the shrapnel wounds whether or not -- just the shrapnel wounds alone, whether it's combat or prisoners, I don't know. I would imagine it's entirely possible to kill somebody with shrapnel in either situation. I wouldn't draw a conclusion from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to look at another report of yours, Liplje 2, that's 2477 65 ter. Let us go briefly through some of the issues. Can we have in e-court -- it was 2477 65 ter, I don't know what the P number is, P4060. Can we have page 2. We can all see what this is about. In item 3 mention is made of the range between 8 and 13 years, 14 and 18, et cetera. Do you know that in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were minors who nowadays they have an organisation of theirs where they fight for their rights?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, are you suggesting they -- they're involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were soldiers aged 14 -- you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under item 4 it says that unfired bullets were recovered which were not contemporary military weapons. Do you know that the Muslims made rifles, they were makeshift rifles, that they made it themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is it a proper question to put this expert, Mr. Karadzic, while complaining of shortage of time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, this is what the report states. I want to point out that a prisoner cannot have bullets on him, and it is a well-known fact that they produced weapons of their own. And I wanted to know if the expert witness was aware of it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have another opportunity to tender those -- prove it possible those facts to the Chamber, but not with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 7 in Serbian your report states that for each and every autopsy it is solely the pathologist conducting it who is responsible for it. And you say that that is the source of evident variations among the different findings and opinions; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following page, "Autopsy Findings," both versions, please, there you say that the remains showed a range of decomposition from relatively well preserved with skin to complete skeletonised. We were able to see that. Under 1 it is stated that in four cases there was identifiable but decomposed brain present. Then under 2, partial skeletonisation, et cetera. Now, this set of remains exhumed at the Dam show a higher degree of decomposition than was the case at other sites. And again, the same conclusion is listed here in respect of which we already said that other possibilities were there as well. So is this what you -- is this the basis on which you said that there were different degrees of decomposition in the bodies retrieved at the various sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Dam site and Liplje were unusual in that they were very coarse material and there seemed to be an awful lot of damage to the material, hence the disarticulation and decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 14 mention is made of bullets that were recovered. In English tracks are of the bullet traces, peri mortem and unfired projectiles -- yes, that's it. Did these issues indicate that this was a combatant?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfired projectiles. [In English] Medium calibre bullet.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. Look, it -- I'm not -- I'm a pathologist, I'm not a ballistics expert. If it's important you should probably get the particular round examined by a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 20, cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us confirm an issue that emerges in all the findings, i.e., that due to the degree of decomposition it was impossible to prove or demonstrate whether the injury was inflicted before or after death and that the pathologists who were trying to ascertain the cause of death used several different terms where the cause of death was -- could not be found, and this was undetermined, unascertained, impossible to ascertain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not find the reference in the original text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, there was a -- some pathologists like different terms. I have used their terms. My term would be "undetermined."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the same putrefying elements be the same with those killed in 1992, 1993, and 1994 as with those who died in 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if I've examined anybody who was -- who died in 1992, 1993, or 1994. Obviously the longer they have been dead the more likely you are to have extensive decomposition, but on the other hand under certain circumstances the body could be quite well preserved. The answer is I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to rule out in respect of all the corpses that you were able to see or your associates were, any other possibilities and say that something dated back to July of 1995, i.e., were you able to rule out the possibility of all the other years?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I've told you I can't just by looking at the bodies determine how long they've been dead for. Sorry, I -- from looking at the bodies alone I couldn't rule out that possibility. It would have to be on the basis of all the other investigation and so forth that you would have to sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Lawrence, thank you. I will not be broaching new topics because I don't have time for them. Thank you very much. I'm sorry that we didn't meet in person, but I had a cold.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, it was put to you on several occasions today, including at transcript page 53, that the individuals in the graves were wearing multiple layers of clothing and therefore it was probable that they died in winter. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter number 3935 in e-court. And if I can go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Doctor, what you're about to see are still images from video footage that was shot in Potocari on 12 or 13 July 1995. I just want you to take a look at some of the individuals in those photos. For example, the man with the number 3 with the shirt, a vest, and a coat.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The same thing, men wearing two or more layers of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can now go to page 8, the next page. If we can blow up that picture and I want you to look at the man on the left wearing the red vest and carrying what appears to be a coat in his right hand. Now, if I can now have 65 ter 4777 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what you're about to see here, Doctor, is a body from the Kozluk grave. These remains have been identified as the same man who we saw on the previous image wearing the red vest who was taken prisoner on 12 or 13 July 1995 in summer. And my question is this: Would the photos that we have just seen assist you or assist the Chamber to explain why there are individuals in Srebrenica-related graves wearing two or three layers of clothing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. What I had to say did not refer to the clothing worn on the upper body but the lower body, trousers, underpants, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. That concludes your evidence, Dr. Lawrence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming again to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're very welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I kindly ask that my associate, Professor Dunjic, be allowed to withdraw as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Yes. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can tender that last photo. It was 65 ter 4777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not the stills from the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, they will all come in as part of the one book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be assigned Exhibit Number P4066. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. If Mr. Nicholls and I can be excused and Ms. Sutherland will be coming in to take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So you suggest to have a short break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Maybe just for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's a matter in the meantime that the Chamber wishes to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps during that break the Court could consider the following, looking at the time remaining today and tomorrow and the estimates for the witnesses, I think it's very clear that we would not be able to come close to completing Mr. Haglund tomorrow. So we -- so perhaps it would be best to release him now and resume or commence his testimony when -- after the winter recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I wanted to raise that with the Court before we did that unilaterally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately that seems to be the case, and if you could convey the Chamber's apologies for his inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime while the next witness is being brought in, there's one matter, administrative matter the Chamber will deal with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On 30th of November, 2011, the accused filed a motion to postpone testimony of Jean Rene Ruez or require viva voce testimony. The accused argues that he does not have the time or resources to review the voluminous material sought to be tendered with Ruez pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Prosecution filed an expedited response on 6th of December, 2011, upon the request of the Chamber, opposing the motion on the basis that in the circumstances the accused will have ample time to review the evidence sought to be presented through Jean Rene Ruez. Now that it is apparent that Ruez's testimony cannot be heard before the winter recess, the motion is now moot. However, the Chamber will, proprio motu, consider whether the accused's request that he be heard live is warranted. The Chamber notes that Mr. Jean Rene Ruez is a special type of witness. His evidence which is primarily visual with a large number of video footage, maps, and photographs will assist the Chamber in familiarising itself with the locations and sites relevant to the Srebrenica component of the case. Tendering his evidence through 92 ter would be counter productive and defeat the very purpose of presenting this evidence in the first place. The Chamber also notes that a large volume of material is sought for admission through this witness. The Chamber, therefore, considers that it is in the interests of justice that Jean Rene Ruez be heard viva voce. The Chamber further notes that in the January and February order of witnesses filed by the Prosecution on 1st of December, 2011, Mr. Richard Butler is listed as a partial Rule 92 ter witness, for whom eight hours of direct examination are already allocated. The subject matter of Mr. Butler's evidence is the command structure of the VRS, and as such at the core of the Prosecution's case and intimately related to the accused's responsibility. The Chamber also notes that for his -- for this witness, more than 500 pages of expert material are expected to be tendered. For these reasons, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice that Mr. Richard Butler be heard viva voce as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, my apology for your inconvenience. I thank you for your indulgence. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Riedlmayer. Can you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: My name is Andras Janos Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your current occupation is the director of the Documentation Center for Islamic Art and Architecture of the Aga Khan Program at the Harvard University; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how long have you been in that employment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: 26 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 13341 on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Riedlmayer, is this the updated CV that you provided to the OTP in November 2011?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court briefly what research work you have done with respect to cultural property during periods of war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Over the last two decades I have done both field research and academic research on the subject of destruction of cultural heritage in the former Yugoslavia, in particular with respect to the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Kosovo. In 1999 and subsequently I conducted field investigations in Kosovo, I also conducted field investigations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as a result you produced reports and you have been qualified as an expert on the destruction of cultural property in six ICTY cases between 2002 and 2010; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I believe so -- no, I believe that was -- yeah, six cases, but I submitted two reports for the Milosevic trial, one for Kosovo, and one for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also testified as an expert before the International Court of Justice in the Bosnia versus Serbia and Montenegro case in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You have authored numerous articles, publications, essays, and reports dealing with the issue of cultural destruction during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and in particular in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and they are listed in my resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are also active in academic societies and a member of a number of professional associations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender Mr. Riedlmayer's CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned Exhibit Number P4067. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you were asked to prepare a report in the context of this case. Can you briefly outline the terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I was requested on 7 April of 2009 to prepare a report for 22 Bosnian municipalities that were listed in Schedule D of the Third Amended Indictment in the Karadzic case, and further I was asked to include in the report the destruction of the national library which was in Schedule D -- Schedule G.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 13340.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Mr. Riedlmayer's expert report. We do have a redacted version of the report which doesn't appear to be uploaded at this moment. It's in the process of being done. The redacted version of the report redacts out the dropped sites listed in Schedule D of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, before we discuss aspects of your report, you wanted to make two corrections to it, and that's in footnote 11. "See note 11 below." Should read: "See note 12 below." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also on the -- in paragraph 47 of the redacted version of the report you wish to insert the words: "(Vogosca municipality)" after the word "Semizovac"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, how do you determine or define cultural heritage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Cultural heritage is a broad term. The -- for the purposes of this report I limited it to two kinds of cultural heritage. One is built heritage and the other one is libraries and archives. Portable heritage was out of the scope of the report; it's a separate subject. What it refers to is the cultural and religious objects that are specific to a particular country or nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I omitted to say that we have also redacted from this report Schedule G3 which was the scheduled site of the national library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, I was told that what we have before us is the redacted version already. And I checked the title of the item in the e-court and it says "redacted version."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the redacted version actually has the words -- as we can see on the first page "and a report on the 25/26 August 1992 shelling of the National and University Library of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo." That text is actually redacted from the version we intend submitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We need a further redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will substitute this version that's in e-court at the moment with the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Mr. Reid had informed me that he had already changed the description of the title but the upload is in the process of being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, I just wish to ask you a few questions in relation to your methodology in relation to the report that you prepared. You mentioned a moment ago that you concentrated on the municipalities which were listed in Schedule D. What -- what work was involved in relation to this report? What exactly was the purpose and your methodology?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: First of all, of the 22 municipalities that were listed in Schedule D, there were six that I had not covered in previous reports for the Tribunal. And so for those six municipalities, I had to compile the documentation de novo. The methodology was as follows. There were a total of 381 sites that were covered. Among them was a subset of the specific indictment sites listed in Schedule D. For the totality of the 381 sites in the municipalities described, I have data-based entries for each site describing the condition of the building and other information. For the indictment sites, I also prepared special formatted entries, meaning outside of the database, which include additional photographs and some additional textual information that wouldn't, for formatting reasons, fit into the database. Would you like me to continue with the methodology questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I was -- my next question for you was: What material did you produce as part of the tasks? And you have mentioned the survey database and also the formatted records. First of all, can you explain briefly what the survey database actually is. You -- in your report you mention how one goes about navigating through, but if you could just briefly explain what the database is.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: What the database is, it is a method of recording in relation to each other both textual information and visual information, photographs, in some cases architectural plans in a searchable database meaning one can sort it by various criteria. The software involved is FileMaker which is a very common database programme. The various fields include everything from the different names by which a particular monument or site is known. The -- its location, including municipality, the town, GPS co-ordinates, questions of whether the monument in question is under special legal protection. And then category to which the monument belongs, is it a church or a mosque or an archive. And then a description of the category of its state, meaning is it in good condition or damaged or destroyed. Then there is a note as to whether the surrounding buildings suffered damage. For this I usually had to refer to photographs taken during or immediately after the war since during my field survey much of the surroundings had been repaired. And then finally there is a more detailed verbal description of the damage and additional information such as information from informants, information from publications, and contemporary media accounts if available, all of which go towards establishing a time-frame as to when this destruction might have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as the survey database is unavailable to be in e-court, but it is on CD-ROM, I wish to put the hard copies of the pages of one of the records on the ELMO just so that you can -- the Trial Chamber can see the type of information which is contained within the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the example that -- that's -- has been selected for you is a Schedule D site and it's the mosque in Biscani from the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: So this is what I was verbally trying to describe. There is the name of the monument in English and in B/C/S, the municipality, the place name, the date of construction, the historical period, official status in this case, none, it was not under special legal protection, and then what kind of monument it was, what kind of setting it was in, and then the building condition. Below it is a description of what the building -- building's condition was and it's based in this case on a site visit as well as on photographs from other sources. So on -- the top photograph shows the interior of the building, the bottom photograph which is taken from the front of the building shows the exterior. The -- each of the entries can run up to three A4 pages when printed out, and this one includes an informant statement. The informant in this case is Ahmet Efendija Rahmanovic who was the head Imam of Prijedor. And I interviewed him, he actually accompanied me to the site, and he mentions the date on which the mosque was destroyed. Below that, if you could move that, please -- no, no, here, the bottom of the page. All the way to the bottom, if that's possible. Well, it's not coming up on the screen but what it is it's a bibliography entry. For every site for which there was published information in the form of records stating its age or published photographs from before the war, I would include that. And in this case also there was none, but I would always include contemporary media accounts that mention the condition of the mosque at a particular date, again to establish when this destruction was occurring. So that's the description.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that additional photographs are contained in the formatted records which we will get to in just a moment, but how many photographs were you able to put into the survey database in relation to each site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The survey database unfortunately could only accommodate two vertical and two horizontal photographs at the maximum. The other technical issue was that since the database had such a large number of entries, the resolution of the photographs had to be kept to a minimum because if you put too much into the database it slows down and ceases functioning. So in the formatted database I was able to use the larger-resolution versions of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the survey database is primarily designed to be -- was that primarily something that was to be used electronically for the searchability aspects of it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The database allows searching and sorting on all fields. So you can easily find, for example, all the churches in a given municipality or all the heavily damaged mosques versus all the partially destroyed mosques and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just before we leave the survey database there was one correction that you wished to make and that was in relation to the entry concerning the "Kramer Selo" mosque in the Rogatica municipality. This entry has the correct town noted and the correction caption under the photograph but the building name is incorrectly cited as "Vragolovi mosque, Dzamija u Vragolovima" and in fact the building name in this entry should read "Kramer Selo mosque, Dzamija u Kramer Selu"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning now to the formatted records, can you -- I think you have explained to the Trial Chamber that they are entries from the survey database in relation to Schedule D sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do the photographs differ between the formatted records and the survey database?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The formatted records in some cases contain additional photographs and as I mentioned before they have better resolution. Otherwise they match.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the report, the survey database, and the formatted records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In one batch or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If they could have separate exhibit numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted. Shall we give the number now? How many of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the redacted report which is 65 ter number 13340, the survey database is 65 ter number 13853, and the formatted records is 65 ter number 13854.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when you tendered the CD you divided these into several parts because of the size of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the survey database is on a separate CD, but the formatted records are actually uploaded in e-court and they have also been redacted, taking out the dropped Schedule D sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the expert report of the Doctor as Exhibit P4068 and survey database as P4069 and the formatted records will be admitted as Exhibit 4070.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, I just want to clarify. You -- for Their Honours' benefit, you were a candidate for a -- for a Ph.D.; was that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I passed the candidacy exam but I decided not to pursue the Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And therefore, I'm referring to you as Mr. Riedlmayer. So therefore, Mr. Riedlmayer, in paragraph 18 which is on page 10 of your report, you make reference to a damage assessment conducted for each site surveyed and you list five levels for the damage and define the criteria for each of these five levels. You call it a five-point assessment scale. The first level on your five-point scale is "good condition." In the municipalities that you studied, did you find any Muslim or Catholic cultural or religious sites in good condition?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you select a number of photos from the formatted records which is now Exhibit P4069?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of sites listed in Schedule D which would help to illustrate the differences in damage in relation to the remaining four levels and other findings in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct as Exhibit 4070.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour, I'm sorry that was -- yeah. If I could have 65 ter number 23553.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These are the photographs that you selected which have been put onto 25 slides, and below each of the photographs is the formatted record's reference number and the name of the site. If we look at the first slide it's captioned "lightly damaged." How does this site fit into that category?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: First let me explain about the damage categories. I found in my research that people were using terms about degree of destruction rather broadly and it was impossible to rely on other people's description of what the damage might be. So I had to devise a series of easily describable clear criteria with which to describe each monument. This is an example of lightly damaged. What you can see here is a mosque. It's located near the former confrontation line in Zvornik municipality. The top of the minaret, the tall spire of the building, has been severed by a projectile impact. And if you look carefully to the right of the minaret part of the roof has been smashed. And it's lightly damaged because the principal structural elements of the building have not been affected. There's a hole in the roof and the top of the minaret is missing, but the four walls appear to be intact and most of the roof is still intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The photograph we're looking at at the moment is of the Vitinica mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Vitinica mosque in Zvornik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The third level on your five-point scale is "heavily damaged." If we move to the next two slides, please, which are captioned "heavily damaged," how does the first of these examples fit into this category?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is also a mosque. It is in Vogosca which is a suburb of Sarajevo. You can see that it is heavily damaged because it has not just the top of the minaret missing, but multiple projectile impacts on the minaret which you can see on the right side of the slide. The top of the minaret is resting on the ground in front of the mosque. The building itself appears to be completely burned out with parts of the walls and parts of the roof missing. It's multiply compromised and thus fits the heavily damaged category.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the next example, the second example, which is the next slide.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a church in a village in Prijedor municipality called Brisevo. On the left in the centre of the forest you see the burned-out church. That's a photo that I took during my field survey in July of 2002. You can see that the roof is missing and the top of the steeple is also missing. I went into the church and I saw char marks on the wall and graffiti in Serbian with Seselj's name and others. The reason I chose the picture on the right is because it was taken immediately after the war. It's a visit by the Catholic bishop of Banja Luka to the church. At that time the floor of the church was still covered with the charred roof tiles and charred woodwork can be seen, remnants of pews and of the roof beams. On the far wall you can see the burned remains of the cross over the altar. So this fits the heavily damaged category again because multiple parts of the building have been compromised. It's completely burned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we move on to the fourth level on your five-point scale I will just note for the record that the first example was the Ugorsko mosque in Vogosca. Sir, the fourth level on the five-point scale is almost destroyed. If we could move, please, to the next two slides which has those captions, how does the first of these examples fit into this category?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: My definition of "almost destroyed" is that several principal parts of the building such as perimeter walls are missing or severely compromised. The building appears beyond repair and would require complete reconstruction but it still has some identifiable elements standing. So here you have a modern mosque in Donji Kamengrad in Sanski Most municipality. You can see that basically three of the walls are gone and the whole roof of the mosque which is a concrete slab is broken and is resting on the ground, but you still have identifiable elements, namely the domes visible. But the building is beyond salvage. So that's why I call it almost destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we look at the second example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The second example is from a village called Ahatovici. It's about 6 kilometres from Sarajevo in Novi Grad municipality. It's a rather more extreme example of the almost destroyed. The only thing left visible and still standing is the stump of the minaret. The rest is just rubble.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, the fifth level on your five-point scale is "completely destroyed." And if we can move to the next three slides, which are captioned "completely destroyed," how does the first of these examples fit into this category?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The first example is actually I would categorise as "almost destroyed." This building was destroyed in two phases. The photograph at left was taken in September of 1992 by Andre Kaiser, a news photographer. It shows the Roman Catholic parish church in Prijedor. And you can see that there is basically one element left standing, an arch, from the church. The woman in front is gathering firewood from the ruins. The church was reportedly blown up in 1995 and so you can see a photo at right. That photo was provided by the Roman Catholic bishop of Banja Luka and was taken from a car. You can see at far right part of the arch, just a tiny fragment of wall, and the rest of it is rubble. On the left is a parish centre, the modern building, which is still standing and it was there when I visited it and I gathered additional photographs and an architectural plan from the parish priest. But I would call this a completely destroyed building by 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can move to the second example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is another Catholic church. It is in Kljuc municipality -- in the town of Kljuc actually. And one has to carefully look at the photographs. These are photographs taken from opposite ends of the same little lane, small street. If you look at the centre of each photograph, there is a tree with a utility pole next to it. That can be seen in both photos. The before photo was published and it dates from the mid-1980s. The building you can see that the left of the church in the pre-war photo is partly visible behind the tree at the far right of the post-war photo. Also I don't know if this presentation allows it to be blown up to enlarge the photo, but if you can do it or take a look at the format -- no, not this one but the post-war photo. Okay. Yes. If you look at that, between the tree and the small pile of stones, you can see the outlines of the foundation. Grass doesn't grow well on top of foundational walls. And so you can actually follow this straight line, it runs parallel to the street. So I also visited the site in 2002, at which point the church had recently been reconstructed. So I can vouch for the fact that the surrounding buildings and the site is still the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And moving to the third example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is in the town of the Rogatica. It's the Carsijska Dzamija or market mosque. And the two photos show the site of the mosque. The photo on the left is actually a photo from 2006 when the mosque was reconstructed. I had a pre-war photo but it dated from the 1960s and wouldn't have shown the modern building behind it. The photo on the right was taken of the site which I've also visited and shows the same building and the empty site where the mosque stood, "completely destroyed" in this case is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I now wish to turn to discuss some of the characteristics of the destruction of sites and the findings in your report. First some of the characteristics. You mentioned -- you've mentioned minarets in a couple of these slides that you've seen before. What is the symbolic value of a minaret?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The function of a minaret is to provide a platform --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if -- sorry, if we could actually go to the next slide. So, sorry, if you could continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, the function of a minaret which you can see on the left here is to provide a place from which the believers can be called to prayer. Muslims are required to pray several times a day. And the symbolic value of it is just like a church steeple in the landscape, it announces the presence of a community, in this case a Muslim community, in a particular location. Further, it refers to the unity of God which is a central tenet of the Muslim faith. Minarets are very useful for purposes of analysing ruined buildings as well for two reasons. One is that in Bosnia they are conventionally placed to the right of the entrance of the building. So it allows one to see the orientation. Mosques are usually directed towards Mecca. So the minaret is to the right of the entrance. The far wall facing the entrance is the prayer niche which faces Mecca which is south/south-east. So on both of these pictures what you are looking at is the south/south-east wall of the mosque, the wall that's away from the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the picture that we're looking at at the moment is the mosque in Kozarusa. So is there anything else that you wish to tell the Court about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I was in Kozarusa again in July of 2002 and it was the tenth anniversary of the destruction of the mosque. It had been reconstructed at that point. So I was given a photo of the mosque that was taken in 1996 which you see at right and I tried to match it up with a photo that showed the same orientation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Other than the minaret missing, what are the characteristics that you wish to highlight with this building?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a mosque at Donja Kamenica-Redzici in Zvornik municipality. And the reason I decided to include this is it shows how a building can be analysed to draw conclusions about how it might have been destroyed. If Your Honours take a look at the body of the minaret, it's more clearly visible on the close-up shot on the right. You can see a large fissure going up. It is my contention that this minaret was blown up with explosives placed inside - that each minaret is hollow and has an internal staircase - so placed inside the staircase, and that the pressure of the explosion blew apart the minaret. I could also confirm this from two other facts. One is that if you look on top the thing that looks like a hat is actually the balcony from high up on the minaret. If this minaret had been destroyed in another fashion, for example, by a projectile, one would expect it to have fallen to one side as you saw in a previous photo. In this case, the explosion was such that it simply landed in the stump of the minaret. The other way I could determine that there had been a large blast is, as you can see, the mosque is built of large blocks of stone and I found these some tens of metres away from the site of the destroyed mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I notice the time if I can go to one more slide to finish this particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would that take?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will have approximately another half an hour -- 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll continue tomorrow at 9.00, and I would appreciate the co-operation of the other Chamber, in particular Tolimir Chamber, for letting us sit tomorrow at Courtroom I. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of December, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.01 p.m.,
